query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Coupling machine-learning interatomic potentials with advanced enhanced-sampling algorithms (e.g., replica exchange metadynamics) can accurately reproduce the free energies of both solid and liquid phases—including all key entropy contributions—at fusion conditions while substantially reducing computational cost compared to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD, particularly in multicomponent high-entropy systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Metallic systems near melting, including elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys, with both solid and liquid phases represented at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Develop and employ ML-based interatomic potentials trained on rigorous ab initio free-energy data coupled with enhanced-sampling techniques to efficiently explore the free-energy landscapes of both phases.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions near melting (e.g., 1000–1600 K) under which both solid and liquid phases coexist, applied across a compositional range from single elements and binaries to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potentials serve as a computational surrogate to rapidly evaluate atomic interactions, while enhanced-sampling mediate complete exploration of configuration space including anharmonic vibrational modes and electron–vibration interactions.
generation.mechanism: By replacing costly on-the-fly ab initio evaluations with pre-trained, high-fidelity ML potentials and ensuring rigorous sampling of the configurational landscape with techniques like replica exchange metadynamics, the method retains accuracy in key free-energy contributions (vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, electron–vibration coupling) while dramatically reducing required computational resources.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach is expected to yield phase free energies and derived thermodynamic observables (e.g., fusion temperatures) with similar fidelity to explicit ab initio MD methods but with an approximate order-of-magnitude reduction in computational time relative to ab initio MD workflows and improved throughput over TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluations that faithfully capture vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling for elemental and binary systems.
generation.boundary: Effective in the temperature range near melting (around 1000–1600 K) and for systems ranging from simple elemental metals and binary alloys to complex high-entropy alloys; uncertainties remain for extreme compositions where ML training data might be sparse.
generation.uncertainty: The exact speedup and fidelity retention in multicomponent high-entropy systems is uncertain due to potential ML interpolation errors and challenges in achieving complete enhanced-sampling in highly complex configurational spaces.

falsification_experiment.design: Implement the ML-enhanced-sampling workflow on a benchmark elemental metal system and a multicomponent high-entropy alloy near their melting temperatures. Compute both solid and liquid phase free energies, fusion temperature, and associated entropy terms. These results will be directly compared against benchmarks from explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD evaluations.
measurements: Phase free energies (for both solid and liquid phases)
Detailed vibrational entropy, anharmonic contributions, and electron–vibration coupling measures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the proposed ML-enhanced-sampling method does not achieve a computational speedup of roughly an order of magnitude while maintaining key free energy differences and derived observables within an acceptable error margin (e.g., ±5% deviation) relative to explicit ab initio MD results, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.

decision.trend: Early computational work on phase transitions in metals started with empirical potentials that, while they were simple and fast, could only yield transition temperatures. Later, direct ab initio molecular‐dynamics studies were developed to compute full free energies (including vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling), which worked very well for elemental and binary systems—but their cost grew prohibitively high when increasing system complexity (as in high‐entropy alloys). Approaches such as TOR-TILD emerged to improve throughput in elemental and binary cases, yet these too stumble on multicomponent systems. Meanwhile, complementary high-throughput and machine-learning based computational screening studies have shown that data‐driven models can begin to capture complex thermodynamic trends, though not yet in a fully free-energy–accurate manner at fusion conditions.
decision.unsolved: A method is still lacking that can accurately calculate the free energies of both solid and fluid phases—including all critical entropy contributions—at conditions near melting for multicomponent high-entropy systems, without resorting to prohibitively expensive ab initio molecular dynamics.
decision.lever: Coupling machine-learning interatomic potentials (trained on rigorous ab initio data) with advanced enhanced-sampling algorithms (for example, replica exchange or metadynamics) to efficiently compute free energies with full anharmonic, vibrational, and electron–vibration contributions
decision.why: Because earlier trends show that explicitly sampling phase space with ab initio MD gives high fidelity but at high cost, and TOR-TILD speeds up simpler systems but struggles with complexity, integrating ML potentials can drastically reduce computational expense while preserving accuracy. Enhanced-sampling methods then ensure that both solid and liquid free-energy landscapes are explored properly. This single, testable hypothesis follows directly from the need to retain all entropy contributions at fusion while extending high-throughput capability across elemental to multicomponent systems.
